The business problem

Guessing tomorrow's solar power, hour by hour

Target variableSolar power for each hour of tomorrow

In megawatts (MW), for the whole CAISO grid.

The ruleOnly what we know at 10 a.m.

CAISO's bids close at 10 a.m. Pacific, the day before.

Picture from our plain-language primer (docs/solar-primer.html in the team repository).

California's grid operator, CAISO, makes tomorrow's power plan today. Before 10 a.m., power companies tell it how much each plant will make, hour by hour. Solar depends on the weather, so it is the hardest number to get right. Too high, and CAISO buys backup power at the last minute. Too low, and power is wasted. [click] Here is our picture. A weather forecast, the time of day and season, and how many panels exist go into our model. It gives one number for each hour of tomorrow. [click] That number is our target variable: solar power for each hour, in megawatts, for the whole CAISO grid. [click] And one rule: we may only use what is known at 10 a.m. [Hand off] Juan David will show the data.
Obtain and qualify the data

Five public sources, each picked for a reason

SourceWhat it gives usWhy we chose it
EIA hourly grid dataActual solar output, hour by hour. Our answer key.Official U.S. data for the whole CAISO area.
Open-MeteoWeather forecasts made 2 days before, at 51 spots in California.Keeps old forecasts, so we use only what was known at 10 a.m.
CAISO day-ahead forecastCAISO's own solar forecast.The grid operator's own guess, a point of comparison.
EIA Form 860MInstalled solar capacity, every month.Solar grew 24%, so 2024 and 2026 need a common scale.
CAISO curtailment reportsSolar that was turned down.EIA measures output after the turn-down, so we need to know when it happened.

How we qualified them: public and free, documented, the same period (Mar 8, 2024 to Oct 17, 2026, 954 days), and usable at 10 a.m.

Weather data by Open-Meteo.com (CC BY 4.0).

[JUAN DAVID, slides 3 to 4. Finish by 3:10] We used five public sources. [click] EIA gives actual solar output hour by hour: our answer key. Open-Meteo gives weather forecasts made two days before, and it keeps old forecasts, so we only use what was known at 10 a.m. CAISO's own forecast is a comparison point. Two smaller files tell us how much solar is installed each month, and how much was turned down. [click] We qualified each source with four questions: is it public, is it documented, does it cover the same period, and could we have had it at 10 a.m.? All five pass, for 954 days.
Prepare the data

From five files to one analysis-ready table

1

Profile

Look at every file

22,896 hourly rows. 226 hours with a gap, under 1%.

2

Organize

Put it on one clock

EIA's hour labels ran 1 hour late until Dec 2, 2025. We corrected them.

3

Join

One row per hour

Five files joined on the hour. Rows counted after every join: always 22,896.

4

Enrich

Add what the model needs

Sun up or not, season, installed capacity that month, a turned-down flag.

5

Segment

Split by time

Earliest days to train and tune. The latest stay locked for the final test.

[click] Five steps, one simple example each. Profile: we looked at every file. For example, 226 of 22,896 hours have a gap, under 1 percent. [click] Organize: everything goes on one clock. EIA's hour labels ran one hour late until December 2, 2025, so we corrected them. [click] Join: five files become one table with one row per hour, and we counted the rows after every join: always 22,896. [click] Enrich: we add what the model needs, like whether the sun is up, the season, and the installed capacity that month. [click] Segment: we split the days in time order. The earliest 763 days are for training and tuning. The latest 191 days stay locked for the final test. [Hand off] Carolina will show what the data looks like.
Descriptive analytics

What the data shows: the sun and the clouds

A typical solar day, by season

Up at 6, peak at noon, done by 8. Summer's peak is 42% higher than winter's.

Cloudier forecast, less solar

Clear forecast: 68% of capacity at midday. Very cloudy: 41%.

Charts made in Python from our hourly table. Training and validation days (Mar 2024 to Apr 9, 2026). Midday = 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. Pacific. Sources: EIA, Open-Meteo.

[CAROLINA, slides 5 to 6. Finish by 5:15] We made these two charts in Python from our table. [click] On the left, the average solar day for each season. Output starts around 6 a.m., peaks at noon and is done by about 8 p.m. In summer the peak is about 42 percent higher than in winter, so the time of day and the season have to be inputs. [click] On the right, we grouped midday hours by how cloudy the forecast said it would be. On clear days solar delivers about 68 percent of installed capacity. On very cloudy days, about 41 percent. So the weather forecast is a useful input: forecast sunshine and real output move closely together, with a correlation of 0.88.
Data quality

How we check quality, and what we did

What we foundHow we found itWhat we did
Clocks off by 1 hourCompared EIA's daily curve with CAISO's own numbers and the sun's position.Moved EIA's labels back 1 hour before Dec 2, 2025. They now match CAISO (correlation 0.998).
Missing hoursCounted the blanks in every file.226 of 22,896 hours, 129 from one weather outage. Flagged and left out of the scores.
Odd values at nightChecked output while the sun was below the horizon.Small negatives set to 0 in a working copy, original kept. 351 odd hours flagged and left out of training.
Turned-down solarCompared CAISO's curtailment reports with EIA output.7.5% of possible solar, up to 24% in April 2026. Flagged, so we can report with and without.

Raw files are never edited. Every fix is code that anyone can re-run.

[click] Quality: how we check, and what we did. Four examples. First, clocks. EIA's hours looked off, so we compared them with CAISO's own numbers and with the sun's position, and found EIA's labels ran one hour late until December 2, 2025. We corrected them in code. [click] Second, gaps. 226 hours of 22,896 are missing, 129 of them from one weather outage. We flag them and leave them out of the scores. [click] Third, odd values at night: small negatives, and a few hours of output in the dark. We set negatives to zero in a working copy, keep the original, and leave the odd hours out of training. [click] Fourth, turned-down solar. When the grid cannot use solar, plants are told to cut output, so measured output is lower than what the sun could have made. It is 7.5 percent overall and up to 24 percent in April 2026. We flag it so we can report with and without. Raw files are never edited: every fix is code anyone can re-run. [Hand off] Raul will close with privacy and delivery risks.
Privacy and delivery risks

Privacy is not a concern. That is the point.

PrivacyOpen data, nothing personal

Public, grid-wide numbers and weather. No customers, no homes, no personal information.

So the whole model can be open: a base, or as is, for anyone's business case.

Delivery risk 1Free weather data has limits

Non-commercial license and a daily cap (we used about 6,500 of 10,000 calls). A business needs the paid tier.

Delivery risk 2Sources can change without notice

EIA changed its clock labels on Dec 2, 2025. Our pull script and timing check can be re-run.

Delivery risk 3Short history

2.6 years: each month appears 2 or 3 times, and our test period has no winter.

Next, in Capstone 3: build and compare forecasting models on this table.
